title: Landing Gear — Nose Wheel Steering Fault on the Runway or during Taxi
abstract: Flight crew procedure for a nose wheel steering fault on the landing roll or during taxi, covering the immediate actions, the use of differential braking and the reporting that lets the fault be found on the ground.

sections.purpose: This entry gives the flight crew procedure for a nose wheel steering fault indicated on the runway or during taxi, and the reporting that lets the fault be found on the ground.
sections.description: A steering fault may appear as an alert, as an unexpected movement of the nose wheel around the commanded angle, or as a late response to a tiller input. The last two are the ones crews find hardest to describe and the ones engineering most needs described accurately. Directional control on the runway remains available through the rudder at speed and through differential braking at low speed, and the aircraft can be taxied without nose wheel steering with a towbar and a tug. The aircraft does not lose directional control when steering is lost, and the crew should resist the reflex to make a large tiller input to recover it, because a system that is hunting will amplify it. After a single channel failure the steering retains the residual authority published in the limitations entry, which is the same on every aircraft in the fleet.
sections.crew_procedure: Maintain directional control with the rudder while the aircraft is above taxi speed and reduce speed on the centreline. Do not make large or rapid tiller inputs to recover a hunting nose wheel. Below taxi speed, use differential braking and asymmetric thrust as necessary to leave the runway. Stop clear and request a tug if the fault persists. Report the fault with the ground speed at which it appeared, whether it was a hunt or a delay, and whether the aircraft had recently had hydraulic work; those three facts determine the isolation path on the ground.

On aircraft at the later steering standard the residual authority after a single channel failure is different and the aircraft will hold a shallower turn than crews may expect.
sections.crew_procedure: Maintain directional control with the rudder while the aircraft is above taxi speed and reduce speed on the centreline. Do not make large or rapid tiller inputs to recover a hunting nose wheel. After a single channel failure the aircraft on the later steering standard holds a shallower turn than crews used to the earlier standard will expect; plan the turn off the runway accordingly and do not add tiller to force it. Below taxi speed, use differential braking and asymmetric thrust as necessary to leave the runway. Stop clear and request a tug if the fault persists. Report the fault with the ground speed at which it appeared, whether it was a hunt or a delay, and whether the aircraft had recently had hydraulic work; those three facts determine the isolation path on the ground.
